name: ERC project state — outdoor + indoor
description: Current state of indoor corridor navigation (MBRA controller, backup fixes, competition-ready) and outdoor GPS navigation (on hold)
type: project
---

## Current Focus: Indoor corridor navigation with MBRA

- **Indoor:** MBRA controller partially working. Backup oscillation fix applied. Competition checkpoints: 45, 480, 761, 821, 1094, 1208, 1345, 1430, 1544, 1638, 1764
- **Outdoor:** On hold — GPS checkpoint navigation with LogoNav, blocked by cars/obstacles on course

---

# INDOOR SYSTEM (Active)

## Competition Run Command
```bash
python live_indoor_runtime.py \
  --checkpoint-steps 45 480 761 821 1094 1208 1345 1430 1544 1638 1764 \
  --auto-advance-checkpoints --send-control --controller mbra --depth-safety
```

## Architecture
See CLAUDE.md in repo root for full documentation.

## Key State (as of 2026-03-25)

### What Works
- CosPlace VPR localization (1865 images, 512-dim, ~95% accuracy)
- MBRA visual navigation controller (follows subgoal images)
- Temporal filtering with continuity penalties
- Forward-only checkpoint skipping
- Depth safety (monocular, stop at 0.25m for MBRA)
- All backup/override mechanisms disabled for MBRA (prevents oscillation)

### Recent Fixes (this session)
1. **MBRA oscillation fix** — disabled recovery backup, RPM stall backup, angular saturation override for MBRA mode. Reversing killed MBRA's 6-frame context.
2. **Jump rejection for MBRA** — resets localizer without reversing
3. **Subgoal hops** — bumped from 4 to 8 for MBRA (needs visual distance between current and goal)
4. **Depth thresholds** — tighter for MBRA (stop=0.25m, slow=0.6m vs stop=0.4m, slow=0.8m for simple)
5. **MBRA warmup** — pre-fills context with copies of first frame (no 2-second stall)
6. **Speed bump** — max_linear 0.24→0.40 for both controllers
7. **Compass disabled** — observation_heading_deg=None for localizer (compass unreliable indoors)

### What Still Needs Work
- MBRA "partially worked" — needs real-world testing to identify remaining issues
- Obstacle avoidance quality (chairs, etc.) depends on MBRA's learned policy + depth safety
- Checkpoint reach detection may need tolerance tuning

## Key Parameters (MBRA mode)
| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| max_subgoal_hops | 8 |
| tick_hz | 3.0 |
| depth_stop_m | 0.25 |
| depth_slow_m | 0.6 |
| MBRA max_linear | 0.40 |
| MBRA max_angular | 0.34 |
| NO_PROGRESS_RESET_TICKS | 10 |

---

# OUTDOOR SYSTEM (On Hold)

## Run Command
```bash
python live_outdoor_runtime.py --mission --send-control --traversability
```

## What Works
- LogoNav (IL_gps) controller, GPS waypoint following
- Reached CP=3/9 in field run
- Depth Anything V2 with auto max_depth
- Semantic risk estimator (SegFormer-B0) built but untested on robot

# Current Session Handoff

Date: 2026-07-19

## Purpose

This is a concise capture of the current working session for transfer with the
rover workspace. It is not a verbatim ChatGPT transcript. The older detailed
conversation records remain available in:

- `chat_handoff.md`
- `chat_session_reconstructed.md`
- `codex_handoff_prompt.md`
- `CONTEXT.md`

## Documentation And Workspace Consolidation

- `live_indoor_runtime.py` is the maintained indoor/no-GPS live runtime.
- The superseded MBRA-first and heavy-recovery variants, plus the obsolete
  `mbra_repo_1` controller adapter, are retained under `legacy/` for
  provenance only.
- The no-GPS operating brief is
  `obsidian_vault/00 Home/Current No-GPS - Read This First.md`.
- Field truth is
  `obsidian_vault/01 Source of Truth/No-GPS Field Trial - Findings.md`.
- `obsidian_vault/` is its own Git repository with a separate remote.
- `mbra_repo_1/` and `nyu-earthrover-main/` are reference workspaces, not the
  current route-repeat runtime path.

## External Samsung SSD

- The external drive was initially detected only as the Ugreen Realtek RTL9210
  enclosure and reported zero capacity.
- After reseating, it is recognized as `/dev/sda`, model `SSD_990_EVO_Plus`,
  with 1 TB decimal capacity (`931.5 GiB` shown by Linux).
- It currently has no partition table, partition, filesystem, label, or mount
  point. It has not been formatted in this session.
- Recommended setup:
  - `GPT + ext4` for Linux-only rover logs, datasets, and model files.
  - `GPT + exFAT` if the SSD will regularly move between Linux, Windows, and
    macOS systems.

## Transfer Archive

The requested workspace archive includes hidden files, Git histories, local
configuration, recordings, model weights, and this handoff. It therefore may
contain secrets such as SDK credentials and Git configuration; keep it private.

167	For industry edge devices, there is no single universal choice:
168	
169	| Format | Typical use | Use it here? |
170	|---|---|---|
171	| `ext4` | Default Linux storage for edge gateways, robots, servers, logs, models | **Best choice** if this SSD stays with this Linux rover computer |
172	| `exFAT` | Portable external drives shared with Linux, Windows, and macOS | Best if you move the SSD between computers |
173	| `NTFS` | Windows-first storage | Only if Windows is the main host |
174	| `FAT32` | Boot/firmware media and old devices | No, it has a 4 GB per-file limit |
175	| `F2FS` | Some flash-focused embedded Linux/Android systems | Valid but not necessary for this USB NVMe SSD |
176	| `XFS` | Large Linux server/video datasets | Good for specialised high-throughput systems, overkill here |
177	| `Btrfs` | Linux snapshots/checksums | Useful only if you specifically want those features |
178	
179	`ext4` is the normal Linux industry baseline because it has journaling, which helps keep filesystem metadata consistent after an unexpected power loss. [Linux ext4 documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v6.6/admin-guide/ext4.html) `F2FS` is specifically designed around flash storage, but it is more common for embedded flash such as eMMC/SD than for a removable NVMe SSD. [Linux F2FS documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v6.10/filesystems/f2fs.html) `exFAT` is simpler and supports large files/devices, but lacks Linux ownership, permissions, and journaling semantics. [Microsoft exFAT specification](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/exfat-specification)
180	
181	For this project, I recommend:
182	
183	- **`GPT + ext4`, label `ROVER_DATA`** if this remains attached to the Linux machine for bags, models, logs, and datasets.
184	- **`GPT + exFAT`, label `ROVER_DATA`** if you will routinely plug it into Windows or macOS machines.

```text
[sda] Read Capacity(10) failed
[sda] 0 512-byte logical blocks: (0 B/0 B)
```

Do **not** format or partition anything. Linux cannot see the SSD itself yet.

Do this in order:

1. Unplug the enclosure and reseat the M.2 SSD fully. Insert it at an angle, push it all the way into the connector, then secure it. Check that a thermal pad or plastic film is not preventing full insertion.
2. Confirm the SSD protocol matches the enclosure. An NVMe enclosure needs an NVMe/M-key drive; an M.2 SATA drive needs SATA support. They look similar but are electrically different.
3. Use another known-good **data** cable directly in a rear motherboard port. The log shows only USB 2 “high-speed,” not SuperSpeed. That may be a bad/low-spec cable, though it alone should not cause a 0-byte drive.
4. Test the Samsung SSD in another NVMe enclosure or a motherboard M.2 slot.
5. Test a known-working NVMe SSD in this Ugreen enclosure.

The test matrix will identify the fault:
- Samsung works elsewhere: Ugreen enclosure, cable, or enclosure firmware/compatibility.
- Another SSD works in Ugreen but Samsung does not: Samsung SSD seating, compatibility, or SSD fault.
- No SSD works in Ugreen: enclosure/cable failure.
- Samsung works nowhere: likely faulty SSD; use warranty/return rather than attempting writes.

[2026-07-19T22:09] USER: what are all the different formatss and what is the widely used one in the industry atleast for edge devices

[2026-07-19T22:10] CODEX: **GPT is not a filesystem.** It is the partition table, like the disk’s map. The format inside the partition is the filesystem.

For industry edge devices, there is no single universal choice:

| Format | Typical use | Use it here? |
|---|---|---|
| `ext4` | Default Linux storage for edge gateways, robots, servers, logs, models | **Best choice** if this SSD stays with this Linux rover computer |
| `exFAT` | Portable external drives shared with Linux, Windows, and macOS | Best if you move the SSD between computers |
| `NTFS` | Windows-first storage | Only if Windows is the main host |
| `FAT32` | Boot/firmware media and old devices | No, it has a 4 GB per-file limit |
| `F2FS` | Some flash-focused embedded Linux/Android systems | Valid but not necessary for this USB NVMe SSD |
| `XFS` | Large Linux server/video datasets | Good for specialised high-throughput systems, overkill here |
| `Btrfs` | Linux snapshots/checksums | Useful only if you specifically want those features |

`ext4` is the normal Linux industry baseline because it has journaling, which helps keep filesystem metadata consistent after an unexpected power loss. [Linux ext4 documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v6.6/admin-guide/ext4.html) `F2FS` is specifically designed around flash storage, but it is more common for embedded flash such as eMMC/SD than for a removable NVMe SSD. [Linux F2FS documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v6.10/filesystems/f2fs.html) `exFAT` is simpler and supports large files/devices, but lacks Linux ownership, permissions, and journaling semantics. [Microsoft exFAT specification](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/exfat-specification)

For this project, I recommend:

- **`GPT + ext4`, label `ROVER_DATA`** if this remains attached to the Linux machine for bags, models, logs, and datasets.
- **`GPT + exFAT`, label `ROVER_DATA`** if you will routinely plug it into Windows or macOS machines.

Do not use `FAT32` for rover recordings or model files.

########## READ THIS FIRST ##########
# Current No-GPS - Read This First

> **Use this note before making any no-GPS route-repeat decision.**
> It is the short version. The evidence is in [[01 Source of Truth/No-GPS Field Trial - Findings]].

## Status: Experimental, Not Cleared For Autonomous Competition Use

| Question | Current answer |
|---|---|
| Does the data pipeline work? | Yes. Manual H5 -> route package works. |
| Does the live runtime connect and send commands? | Yes. |
| Does the rover move? | Yes. |
| Has it completed a reliable autonomous taught-route repeat? | **No.** |
| Is `smoke_run01_c` a deployment route? | **No.** It is the best reference/coverage candidate. |
| Can existing bags replay human teleop exactly? | **No.** Their `controls` stream is empty. |

## Problem Contract

This is a **no-GPS, rough-terrain, differential-drive, visual teach-and-repeat**
problem. It is not the older GPS mission stack and it is not generic
exploration. The rover must localize against a manually taught front-camera
route, choose a nearby graph subgoal, and traverse rocks without losing the
route corridor.

## Current Reference Decision

- strongest original teach recording: `run_01_1521.h5`
- main coverage/reference candidate: `smoke_run01_c` (`126` frames,
  `target_step=125`)
- best post-processing comparison: `run_01_1521_pp_v3` (`15` frames,
  `target_step=14`)

`smoke_run01_c` remains the primary reference because it has useful route
coverage. The cleaner-looking 15-frame derivative is a comparison experiment,
not a replacement deployment route. For this rover, route quality means
motion-rich coverage, visual progression, and useful relocalization evidence;
it does not mean the prettiest video alone.

## What We Know

- GPS is unusable in this session: `(1000, 1000)` is a placeholder.
- The no-GPS runtime is front-camera-only. Rear camera is not fused.
- Rough-terrain prepared-route runs use the adaptive pursuit controller.
- Route heading is disabled by default in rough-terrain launches because it was unreliable in field tests.
- Rocks, tilt, weak visual matching, and recovery loops are the current limiting system, not missing CLI plumbing.

## What Failed In The Field

- Localization repeatedly remained around startup steps `0`, `1`, or `8`.
- Confidence was moderate, not decisive, and did not yield sustained graph-step progression.
- The runtime repeatedly entered scan/probe recovery loops.
- Stronger forward commands moved the rover but did not prove that it was following the taught route.

## The Only Valid Next Goal

Prove one **short, repeatable hardware-in-the-loop segment** on the exact same physical route:

1. Start position visually matches the reference start.
2. Localization remains within the expected route corridor.
3. Graph step advances meaningfully.
4. The rover does not cycle through repeated scan/probe recovery.
5. Repeat the segment successfully at least once.

Do not jump from “the rover moves” to “the rover can run the final route.”

## Read Next

- Evidence and exact logs: [[01 Source of Truth/No-GPS Field Trial - Findings]]
- Controller design and limits: [[01 Source of Truth/Offroad Controller - Full Story]]
- Full project narrative: [[erc3_full_documentation]]

########## FIELD TRIAL FINDINGS ##########
# No-GPS Field Trial - Findings

> **Purpose:** Evidence record for the rough-terrain no-GPS route-repeat tests.
> **Authority:** This note records what the rover actually did. It overrides optimistic wording elsewhere; active code remains the source for exact behavior.

## Bottom Line

The no-GPS branch has a usable data and software pipeline, but it has **not** demonstrated a reliable autonomous repeat of the taught route on the real terrain.

What is true:

- manual recording, route preparation, front-camera localization, and command sending work;
- the rover does move under `--send-control`;
- rough-terrain recovery and adaptive-pursuit code are implemented;
- current field runs repeatedly failed to make sustained graph-step progress.

This is therefore an experimental route-repeat system, not a proven competition-ready autonomy capability.

## Hardware And Sensor Reality

- GPS was unusable in the session: telemetry reported `(1000, 1000)`.
- The live no-GPS runtime uses **front camera only** through `/v2/front`.
- Rear-camera data is not part of the live localization or route-following path.
- The rover is differential drive and operates on uneven, rocky terrain; body tilt materially changes both image appearance and traction.

## What Was Tested

The tests used `data/manual_routes/smoke_run01_c` as the reference candidate, normally with:

- `--rough-terrain`
- `--send-control`
- front-camera-only live input
- startup-step hints near the expected start

We also tested route-heading guidance, no-route-heading operation, constrained startup localization, forward-biased recovery, adaptive pursuit, and more aggressive terrain settings.

## Observed Field Behavior

The important log signatures were consistent across attempts:

- localization commonly stayed near steps `0`, `1`, or `8` while confidence remained roughly `0.49-0.59`;
- `relocalize_scan`, `relocalize_probe_forward`, and recovery cycles repeated without sustained route progression;
- route-heading / compass guidance could increase heading error instead of reducing it, so it was disabled for the no-GPS branch;
- tight startup corridors prevented unsafe global jumps but did not create a visual match where the live start disagreed with the teach reference;
- at tilt around `14-22` degrees, cautious crawl commands were often too weak to cross rocks, while stronger probes still did not establish durable localization progress.

This means a lack of graph-step progress is not proof that the rover physically did nothing. It is evidence that the perception, reference route, and recovery state machine did not agree on where it was or how it should continue.

## Changes Made During The Tests

The current code incorporates these hardening changes:

- `src/adaptive_pursuit_controller.py` provides the rough-terrain controller family.
- `scripts/run_prepared_route.py --rough-terrain` selects that controller.
- The live runtime uses front camera only.
- rough-terrain prepared-route launches default to no route-heading guidance;
  `--use-route-heading` is an explicit opt-in because the compass/route-heading
  relation was unreliable in these tests.
- Startup localization can be constrained with a step hint, radius, and lock period.
- Corridor localization no longer silently falls through to a global match when a constrained window has no valid candidates.
- Rough-terrain recovery is forward-biased rather than repeatedly reversing on rocks.
- Tilt, RPM, confidence, and no-progress state affect command generation.

These are code changes, not field validation. The field evidence above still governs the maturity claim.

## Route And Recording Evidence

| Artifact | Role | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `run_01_1521.h5` | strongest original teach recording | best coverage candidate, not a proven autonomous route |
| `smoke_run01_c` | 126-frame reference, `target_step=125` | main comparison route; unproven in field repeat |
| `run_01_1521_pp_v3` | 15-frame post-processing experiment, `target_step=14` | useful selector experiment; too sparse for primary use |
| `run_02_1537.h5` | alternate teach recording | weaker: dark segment and poor tail |
| `run_03_1551.h5` | alternate teach recording | usable comparison only |
| `run_05_clean_teach.h5` | later recording | unreviewed; no route package or validation verdict yet |

The existing manual recordings have `controls: 0`. They contain video and telemetry but not the original teleoperation command stream, so exact command replay cannot be reconstructed from them.

## Decision Rule Before Another Autonomous Attempt

Do not treat a long autonomous no-GPS run as justified until a controlled hardware-in-the-loop test demonstrates all of the following on the same physical route:

1. startup localization stays in the expected corridor without a manual step hint being wrong;
2. graph step advances across a meaningful route segment;
3. the controller does not enter repeated scan/probe loops;
4. command strength is sufficient for the terrain without increasing unsafe tilt;
5. a short repeat can be reproduced, not merely observed once.

Until then, the honest operational position is that this branch is a promising prototype and its safest role is supervised evaluation, not unattended final-competition execution.

## Related Notes

- [[00 Home/Current No-GPS - Read This First]]
- [[01 Source of Truth/Offroad Track - Full Story]]
- [[01 Source of Truth/Offroad Controller - Full Story]]
- [[03 Personal Notes/Current Truth]]
- [[04 Runs and Failures/Run Outcomes]]

name: ERC project state — no-GPS teach-and-repeat is the active branch
description: Current state of the rover project — the no-GPS rough-terrain teach-and-repeat branch (active, unproven), with indoor MBRA and outdoor GPS both retired

As of 2026-04-27 (last field session; verified still true 2026-08-06) the active
problem is **no-GPS, rough-terrain, differential-drive visual teach-and-repeat**,
front camera only. Both earlier systems are historical:

- **Outdoor GPS/LogoNav** — dead end for the current bot. On 2026-04-22 the SDK
  returned `latitude=1000, longitude=1000` (placeholder), so `live_outdoor_runtime.py`
  cannot run. Not a code bug.
- **Indoor MBRA corridor navigation** — superseded. `live_indoor_runtime_mbra.py`,
  `live_indoor_runtime_recovery.py`, `src/mbra_local_controller.py` moved to `legacy/`.

## Active path

`scripts/run_prepared_route.py` → `live_indoor_runtime.py` →
`src/adaptive_pursuit_controller.py`. Rough-terrain runs default to the `adaptive`
controller and to `--no-route-heading` (compass/route heading made heading error
worse in the field).

Reference route: `data/manual_routes/smoke_run01_c` (126 frames, target_step=125),
built from `recordings/manual_flag_collection/2026-04-22/run_01_1521.h5`.

## Status: implemented, NOT field-proven

Pipeline works (record → postprocess → route package → localize → send commands),
rover moves, but no reliable autonomous route repeat was ever demonstrated.
Field failure signature: `cur` stuck at step 0/1/8, conf ~0.49-0.59, repeated
`relocalize_scan` / `relocalize_probe_forward` loops.

## Known open items (2026-08-06)

- All no-GPS work is **uncommitted** — last commit `ff81836` is 2026-04-17, and
  2 commits are unpushed. `data/` and `recordings/` are gitignored, so route
  packages and bags exist only on this machine + the SSD backup zip.
- `recordings/run_05_clean_teach.h5` (160 frames) was never turned into a route package.
- Recorder writes a `controls` dataset but it is always empty — teleop goes through
  the browser / `keyboard_control.py`, not the recorder, so taught commands can
  never be replayed.

See [[codex_collaboration]] and [[startup_sequence]]. Authoritative in-repo docs:
`obsidian_vault/00 Home/Current No-GPS - Read This First.md` and
`obsidian_vault/01 Source of Truth/No-GPS Field Trial - Findings.md`.

```bash
sudo fuser -k 8000/tcp 2>/dev/null; cd ~/Desktop/rover/ERC-3-earthrover-challenge/earth-rovers-sdk && conda activate erv && hypercorn main:app --reload
```

Terminal 2 — start mission:

Terminal 3 — single target step:

---
name: ERC project state — outdoor + indoor
description: Current state of indoor corridor navigation (MBRA controller, backup fixes, competition-ready) and outdoor GPS navigation (on hold)
type: project
---

## Current Focus: Indoor corridor navigation with MBRA

- **Indoor:** MBRA controller partially working. Backup oscillation fix applied. Competition checkpoints: 45, 480, 761, 821, 1094, 1208, 1345, 1430, 1544, 1638, 1764
- **Outdoor:** On hold — GPS checkpoint navigation with LogoNav, blocked by cars/obstacles on course

---

# INDOOR SYSTEM (Active)

## Competition Run Command
```bash
python live_indoor_runtime.py \
  --checkpoint-steps 45 480 761 821 1094 1208 1345 1430 1544 1638 1764 \
  --auto-advance-checkpoints --send-control --controller mbra --depth-safety
```

## Architecture
See CLAUDE.md in repo root for full documentation.

## Key State (as of 2026-03-25)

### What Works
- CosPlace VPR localization (1865 images, 512-dim, ~95% accuracy)
- MBRA visual navigation controller (follows subgoal images)
- Temporal filtering with continuity penalties
- Forward-only checkpoint skipping
- Depth safety (monocular, stop at 0.25m for MBRA)
- All backup/override mechanisms disabled for MBRA (prevents oscillation)

### Recent Fixes (this session)
1. **MBRA oscillation fix** — disabled recovery backup, RPM stall backup, angular saturation override for MBRA mode. Reversing killed MBRA's 6-frame context.
2. **Jump rejection for MBRA** — resets localizer without reversing
3. **Subgoal hops** — bumped from 4 to 8 for MBRA (needs visual distance between current and goal)
4. **Depth thresholds** — tighter for MBRA (stop=0.25m, slow=0.6m vs stop=0.4m, slow=0.8m for simple)
5. **MBRA warmup** — pre-fills context with copies of first frame (no 2-second stall)
6. **Speed bump** — max_linear 0.24→0.40 for both controllers
7. **Compass disabled** — observation_heading_deg=None for localizer (compass unreliable indoors)

### What Still Needs Work
- MBRA "partially worked" — needs real-world testing to identify remaining issues
- Obstacle avoidance quality (chairs, etc.) depends on MBRA's learned policy + depth safety
- Checkpoint reach detection may need tolerance tuning

## Key Parameters (MBRA mode)
| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| max_subgoal_hops | 8 |
| tick_hz | 3.0 |
| depth_stop_m | 0.25 |
| depth_slow_m | 0.6 |
| MBRA max_linear | 0.40 |
| MBRA max_angular | 0.34 |
| NO_PROGRESS_RESET_TICKS | 10 |

---

# OUTDOOR SYSTEM (On Hold)

## Run Command
```bash
python live_outdoor_runtime.py --mission --send-control --traversability
```

## What Works
- LogoNav (IL_gps) controller, GPS waypoint following
- Reached CP=3/9 in field run
- Depth Anything V2 with auto max_depth
- Semantic risk estimator (SegFormer-B0) built but untested on robot

## Current Focus: Indoor corridor navigation with MBRA

- **Indoor:** MBRA controller partially working. Backup oscillation fix applied. Competition checkpoints: 45, 480, 761, 821, 1094, 1208, 1345, 1430, 1544, 1638, 1764
- **Outdoor:** On hold — GPS checkpoint navigation with LogoNav, blocked by cars/obstacles on course

---

# INDOOR SYSTEM (Active)

## Competition Run Command
```bash
python live_indoor_runtime.py \
  --checkpoint-steps 45 480 761 821 1094 1208 1345 1430 1544 1638 1764 \
  --auto-advance-checkpoints --send-control --controller mbra --depth-safety
```

## Architecture
See CLAUDE.md in repo root for full documentation.

## Key State (as of 2026-03-25)

### What Works
- CosPlace VPR localization (1865 images, 512-dim, ~95% accuracy)
- MBRA visual navigation controller (follows subgoal images)
- Temporal filtering with continuity penalties
- Forward-only checkpoint skipping
- Depth safety (monocular, stop at 0.25m for MBRA)
- All backup/override mechanisms disabled for MBRA (prevents oscillation)

### Recent Fixes (this session)
1. **MBRA oscillation fix** — disabled recovery backup, RPM stall backup, angular saturation override for MBRA mode. Reversing killed MBRA's 6-frame context.
2. **Jump rejection for MBRA** — resets localizer without reversing
3. **Subgoal hops** — bumped from 4 to 8 for MBRA (needs visual distance between current and goal)
4. **Depth thresholds** — tighter for MBRA (stop=0.25m, slow=0.6m vs stop=0.4m, slow=0.8m for simple)
5. **MBRA warmup** — pre-fills context with copies of first frame (no 2-second stall)
6. **Speed bump** — max_linear 0.24→0.40 for both controllers
7. **Compass disabled** — observation_heading_deg=None for localizer (compass unreliable indoors)

### What Still Needs Work
- MBRA "partially worked" — needs real-world testing to identify remaining issues
- Obstacle avoidance quality (chairs, etc.) depends on MBRA's learned policy + depth safety
- Checkpoint reach detection may need tolerance tuning

## Key Parameters (MBRA mode)
| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| max_subgoal_hops | 8 |
| tick_hz | 3.0 |
| depth_stop_m | 0.25 |
| depth_slow_m | 0.6 |
| MBRA max_linear | 0.40 |
| MBRA max_angular | 0.34 |
| NO_PROGRESS_RESET_TICKS | 10 |

- LogoNav (IL_gps) controller, GPS waypoint following
- Reached CP=3/9 in field run

content.text:
I read the Codex history — one long-running thread in `~/.codex/sessions/` (64 MB, `2026-03-22` → `2026-08-06`, ~500 exchanges), cross-checked against the repo's own source-of-truth notes and the actual files on disk.

Here's what happened and where you actually are.

## The arc — the project pivoted twice

**Phase 1 (Mar 22 – Apr 17): outdoor GPS marathon.** LogoNav + OSM routing + IMU/depth/semantic safety in `live_outdoor_runtime.py`. The marathon run failed. On Apr 22 Codex did a vulnerability review and fixed real bugs: `semantic_yield` was reading `command` before it was assigned, "hard stop" wasn't hard because EMA smoothing blended forward motion back in, hard stops auto-resumed after 2 ticks, `ALIGN` could spin forever. Also added `--log-dir` run logging.

**Phase 2 (Apr 22, one afternoon): GPS turned out to be dead.** `/data` returned `latitude: 1000, longitude: 1000` — a placeholder. Not your bug. The outdoor runtime correctly refuses to run. You said "there will be no GPS, we need to look for flags," and the whole problem changed.

**Phase 3 (Apr 22 – Apr 27): no-GPS visual teach-and-repeat.** This is the current system. Built from scratch in about five sessions:

- `scripts/record_sdk_session.py` — record a manual drive to H5
- `scripts/postprocess_teach_bag.py` — score/clean frames, keep motion-rich episodes
- `scripts/prepare_manual_route.py` — bag → dataset → CosPlace DB → nav graph
- `scripts/run_prepared_route.py` — one-command launcher
- `src/adaptive_pursuit_controller.py` — curvature-tracking controller replacing the align-then-drive one

Real bugs found and fixed along the way: compass heading sign was inverted (it turned the *wrong way*), the localizer silently fell back to global search when the startup corridor had no candidates (that's why it teleported to step 54/87/125), and the startup corridor only filtered the top-K global matches instead of searching the full route.

## Where it actually stands

The pipeline works. The rover moves. **It has never completed a reliable autonomous route repeat.**

The Apr 27 field log is the honest picture: `cur` stuck at step 1 or 8, confidence flat at 0.49–0.59, endlessly cycling `relocalize_scan` → `relocalize_probe_forward`. Codex's last word before you stopped: *"this is not a control-tuning problem anymore — the stack is not acquiring the taught path from this start pose."*

After Apr 27 there was **no more field work** — May 20 was a GitHub question, Jul 16 was documentation cleanup, Jul 19–20 was the SSD backup, Aug 6 was "hiu".

## What we need to do

Your own repo already states the gate, in `Current No-GPS - Read This First.md`: prove **one short, repeatable hardware-in-the-loop segment** on the same physical route — start pose matches the reference, localization stays in corridor, graph step advances, no scan/probe cycling, and it repeats at least once. Everything else is downstream of that.

## Three things I noticed that aren't in any note

1. **None of the no-GPS work is committed.** Last commit is `ff81836` from Apr 17 — *before* the entire phase-3 build. `src/adaptive_pursuit_controller.py`, all five scripts, and the field-trial notes are untracked. Two commits are also unpushed. This is the biggest risk on the board.

2. **The route packages and bags are gitignored.** `data/` and `recordings/` are both in `.gitignore`, so `smoke_run01_c` and `run_01_1521.h5` exist only on this machine and inside the 18 GB SSD zip. If the machine dies, the reference route dies with it.

3. **`run_05_clean_teach.h5` was never used.** You recorded it Apr 24 (160 frames, front-only) and then the conversation moved to post-processing and never came back. It was meant to be the *clean* teach bag — the one recorded deliberately for repeat, unlike `run_01` which was flag-collection footage. That's a free experiment sitting on disk.

Also worth knowing: the recorder has a `controls` dataset but it's always empty, because teleop goes browser → SDK directly and never through the recorder. That's why "just replay the commands that recorded the bag" was impossible. It's fixable if you want that option.

I've updated my memory — the old notes still said "indoor MBRA is the active focus," which has been wrong since April.

Want me to start with the git safety net (commit + push the phase-3 work, and decide what to do about the ignored route data), or go straight at the localization problem?

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF' && git log -1 --stat --format='%h %s' | head -3
Add no-GPS rough-terrain teach-and-repeat branch

The bot's SDK returns placeholder GPS (1000, 1000), so the outdoor
mission runtime cannot run. The active problem is now no-GPS,
rough-terrain, differential-drive visual teach-and-repeat using the
front camera only.

Pipeline (record -> clean -> route package -> repeat):
- scripts/record_sdk_session.py     manual drive -> H5 bag, front-only
- scripts/postprocess_teach_bag.py  score frames, keep motion episodes
- scripts/prepare_manual_route.py   bag -> dataset -> CosPlace DB -> graph
- scripts/run_prepared_route.py     launcher for the above
- scripts/visualize_manual_route.py route contact sheets

Control:
- src/adaptive_pursuit_controller.py replaces align-then-drive with
  curvature tracking, pivot fallback, and progress-aware speed scaling.
  Rough-terrain runs default to it, and to --no-route-heading.

Fixes found during field tests:
- compass heading sign was inverted, so the rover turned the wrong way
- corridor localizer silently fell back to global search when the
  constrained startup window had no candidates, causing step teleports
- startup corridor now searches the full route then filters to the
  allowed window instead of filtering the top-K global matches
- tilt estimation from IMU; rough-terrain recovery is forward-biased

Outdoor runtime hardening from the earlier marathon review is included:
semantic_yield now uses the current tick's command, stop-class commands
bypass EMA smoothing, hard stops require operator confirmation in
marathon/night-safe, IMU calibration gates nav-ready.

Superseded MBRA and heavy-recovery runtimes moved to legacy/.

Status: implemented, NOT field-proven. No reliable autonomous route
repeat has been demonstrated. See
obsidian_vault/01 Source of Truth/No-GPS Field Trial - Findings.md

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

## ✅ Main repo — pushed

`vivekmattam02/ERC-3-earthrover-challenge` → `45a37cf..c166e98` on `main`, 3 commits:

That includes `src/adaptive_pursuit_controller.py`, all five pipeline scripts, the localizer/controller bug fixes, `legacy/`, the `postprocessed/` evidence, and all 57 vault files.

Nothing sensitive went up — `.env` stayed ignored, and a scan for tokens/keys across every added and modified file came back clean.

## ⚠️ Vault repo — NOT pushed, and you should look at this

`vivekmattam02/obsidian` **is not your rover vault anymore.** It's a different project:

```
3462c7a  2026-04-22  Flatten vault structure to make repo root the vault
3b3a437  2026-04-22  Remove redundant old vault
0b56d20  2026-04-22  Initial commit: Active Perception architecture and Phase 1 core math
```

24 files — `00 Active Perception Bible.md`, EKF/tracker/data-association Python, ROS 2 and Jetson notes, `vivek_resume.pdf`. The two histories have **no common ancestor at all**, and my `git fetch` reported a *forced update*.

Reading the dates: your rover vault went up around Apr 17, then on Apr 22 the Active Perception vault was force-pushed over it, wiping the rover vault from that remote.

So pushing your local vault there is only possible with `--force`, which would destroy those 3 commits of Active Perception work. **I didn't do that.** I committed your vault changes locally instead — `e1ba472`, safe on disk, nothing sent anywhere.

Your rover vault content is not at risk either way: it's already on GitHub inside the main repo at `obsidian_vault/`.

Three ways out, whenever you want to pick one:
- **New repo** — push the rover vault to e.g. `obsidian-rover`, leave Active Perception alone (cleanest)
- **Drop the separate repo** — the main repo already tracks every vault file; you'd just delete `obsidian_vault/.git` and stop double-committing
- **Force-push anyway** — only if that Active Perception work is backed up elsewhere; I'd want you to confirm that explicitly first

Worth knowing regardless: the vault being tracked in *both* repos means every vault edit needs two commits. That's how the divergence went unnoticed for three months.

only. Both earlier systems are historical:
